blindSummary:
This capital-region state/province tracks the country as a whole closely for a traveller, because its negative and positive factors largely cancel. On the negative side, the capital agglomeration and urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 55% of anti-LGBT offences for 43% of the population — a rate of 9 per 100,000, more than double the rural figure of 4 (2025 update: 54% for 43%, still 9 per 100,000 against the rural 4 and a rate of 7 for the country as a whole). The 2025 pride march was mobilised under a heavy police frame: a self-described "gay patriot" collective sought to march with the backing of the centrally appointed regional authority, an umbrella LGBTI organisation threatened to cancel if it participated, and participants reported the march "is becoming a sensitive event". A visitor attending Pride encounters organisational tension and a security apparatus that signals vulnerability even as it protects.

On the positive side, the 9-per-100k rate is heavily inflated by reporting propensity, community visibility, dedicated police liaison desks and the density of associations — more incidents are recorded and responded to, which is not the same as a visitor being at greater risk; the capital alone records 22 per 100,000, but an official note cautions that offences there also involve non-residents (commuters and tourists). This state/province has the country's densest trans support infrastructure and the largest community, giving a discovered visitor the best documented odds of institutional help and social buffer anywhere on the mainland.

Where the authorities in another state/province actively banned assembly, the response to Pride here was protective if tense; and an official caveat in the sources warns explicitly against reading the capital's high recorded rates as the capital being dangerous.
blindSourceSummaries: The interior ministry's statistics service, rapid crime-safety note of May 2025: 4,800 recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in the country in 2024 (+5% on 2023; crimes and offences up 14% a year since 2016); only about 4% of victims file complaints; acts concentrate in urban units over 200,000 inhabitants, notably the capital — whose rate, 22 per 100,000 against the country's 7, the note attributes partly to non-resident victims and commuters; recorded victims are over 70% men.

An inter-ministerial statistics briefing of May 2026: 4,900 recorded anti-LGBT+ offences in 2025 (+2%); urban units over 200,000 inhabitants concentrate 54% of offences for 43% of the population; their rate is 9 per 100,000 against 4 in rural communes and 7 for the country as a whole; accused are 83% men, victims mostly young men.
blindOutOfScope: Ordinary urban crime (pickpocketing, theft) and the density of protests and strikes in the capital region affect all travellers and do not move trans-specific risk.
blindTangential: Recorded anti-LGBT+ crime here is predominantly homophobic — over 70% of victims are men — so the metro concentration figures describe the enforcement environment trans visitors share with LGB travellers rather than trans-specific victimisation counts.
